1	# Skill body grammar - exact syntax
2	
3	The literal, copyable syntax behind the "Body grammar" section of
4	[SKILL.md](../SKILL.md), which holds the judgement (when to inject, why a
5	fallback, what to bound). The literals live here because a SKILL.md body is
6	preprocessed at load and a reference file, read on demand, never is.
7	
8	> Behaviour marked "observed" was seen by loading probe skills headless on
9	> Claude Code 2.1.295. Everything else is from the skills docs
10	> (https://code.claude.com/docs/en/skills, checked 2026-10-09), which now
11	> document most of what used to be observation only.
12	
13	## Where the grammar applies
14	
15	| File | Preprocessed? |
16	| --- | --- |
17	| `SKILL.md` body (and `.claude/commands/*.md`) | Yes - directives run, placeholders substitute |
18	| A skill's `references/` and other supporting files | No - plain text when Read |
19	| Subagent bodies in `.claude/agents/` or `~/.claude/agents/` | No - arrives as literal text (observed) |
20	| Subagent bodies in a plugin's `agents/` | Only the plugin path variables expand (which: the plugin-agent note in `claude-lint fields agent`); directives and argument placeholders stay literal (observed) |
21	| Rule files and CLAUDE.md | No - arrives as literal text |
22	| A skill synced from claude.ai, run on your machine | Directives never run; `@` references and some variables stay literal |
23	
24	## Dynamic context injection
25	
26	The command runs locally before the model sees the skill; its output replaces
27	the directive. Substitution is one pass over the original file: output is
28	inserted as plain text and is not re-scanned, so a command cannot emit a
29	directive for a later pass.
30	
31	Inline - an exclamation mark immediately followed by a backtick-quoted command.
32	It is recognised only at the start of a line or straight after whitespace; glued
33	to another character, as in ``KEY=!`cmd` ``, it is left as text and does not
34	run:
35	
36	```text
37	Current branch: !`git branch --show-current 2>/dev/null || echo "no data: not a git repository"`
38	```
39	
40	Fenced, for multi-line - a code fence whose opening line is three backticks
41	followed by an exclamation mark:
42	
43	````text
44	```!
45	git status --short 2>/dev/null | head -30 | grep . || echo "no data: clean tree or not a git repository"
46	git log --oneline -5 2>/dev/null || echo "no data: no commits yet"
47	```
48	````
49	
50	### The fallback pattern
51	
52	A command that exits non-zero aborts the whole skill invocation, not just its
53	own directive: Claude never sees the body, and the user gets
54	`Shell command failed for pattern "..."` with the output under `[stderr]`
55	(docs; observed with an exit code of 3). The one carve-out is exit code 1 from
56	search and comparison commands such as `grep` and `diff`, which is treated as a
57	normal result. With the default bash shell stderr is merged into the injected
58	text. Silencing it with `2>/dev/null` does not change the exit status, so that
59	alone still aborts (observed). Silence it and chain an echo so the skill
60	degrades into something actionable instead of failing to load:
61	
62	```text
63	!`cmd 2>/dev/null || echo "no data: <reason>"`
64	```
65	
66	The docs' own idiom for a command expected to exit non-zero is a trailing
67	`|| true`; the echo form is the same guard with a reason attached. `claude-lint`
68	rule SK005 flags a directive with neither.
69	
70	### Reading an environment variable
71	
72	Ordinary shell variables written in body text (`$VAR`) are not expanded. Read
73	one with `printenv`, pre-approved for that one name:
74	
75	```text
76	allowed-tools: Bash(printenv DEPLOY_ENV)
77	
78	!`printenv DEPLOY_ENV 2>/dev/null || echo "no data: DEPLOY_ENV is not set"`
79	```
80	
81	The obvious `echo $VAR` does not load: an echo that expands a variable fails the
82	permission check, quoted or not, and a `Bash(echo *)` entry does not rescue it
83	(observed; only `$HOME`, and `$USER` inside double quotes, got through without
84	blanket `Bash`).
85	
86	### Bounding the output
87	
88	The cap goes in the command itself, as a pipe into `head`. That pipe also
89	guards the exit status - a trailing `head` succeeds even when the command
90	before it failed - but for the same reason a fallback chained after it never
91	fires, and the body gets an empty result. Put `grep .` after `head` to turn
92	empty output into the fallback (it also drops blank lines). Each command also
93	runs under the Bash tool's default 2-minute timeout:
94	
95	```text
96	!`git diff --stat 2>/dev/null | head -40 | grep . || echo "no data: no diff"`
97	!`gh pr view --json title,body 2>/dev/null | head -c 4000 | grep . || echo "no data: no PR for this branch"`
98	```
99	
100	The second needs `allowed-tools: Bash(gh pr view *)`; `git diff`, `head` and
101	`grep` pass as read-only. Do not put the fallback inside the pipe by wrapping
102	it in parentheses or braces - `(cmd || echo ...) | head` fails the permission
103	check unless the skill has blanket `Bash` (all observed on 2.1.295).
104	
105	## Argument substitutions
106	
107	| Form | Substitutes |
108	| --- | --- |
109	| `$ARGUMENTS` | All arguments as typed |
110	| `$ARGUMENTS[N]` | The Nth argument, 0-based (`$ARGUMENTS[0]` is the first) |
111	| `$N` | Shorthand for the same (`$0`, `$1`, ...) |
112	| `$name` | A named positional declared in `arguments` frontmatter (`arguments: [issue, branch]` or `arguments: issue branch` gives `$issue` and `$branch`) |
113	
114	If no placeholder of any of these kinds receives an argument, the arguments are
115	appended to the end as `ARGUMENTS: <value>`.
116	
117	Indexed arguments use shell-style quoting: `/my-skill "hello world" second`
118	makes `$0` expand to `hello world`. An indexed placeholder with no argument at
119	its position stays in the text unchanged (`$3` stayed `$3`, observed); a named
120	placeholder with no argument becomes an empty string. An argument value that

- Frontmatter is read only when `---` is the file's first line; YAML that does not parse leaves the skill loaded with no fields set.

trajectory.body:
file_path: skills/skill-args-guide/SKILL.md
content:
---
description: Explains how arguments reach a skill and what each placeholder becomes - the ARGUMENTS placeholder, numbered placeholders such as 0 and 1, named placeholders declared in arguments frontmatter - and how to escape them. Load this before writing, reviewing, debugging or advising on any skill that takes arguments, even a small one. Without it, people drop a bare ARGUMENTS placeholder into an example and it gets substituted at load, expect a numbered placeholder with no matching argument to be filled, assume a doubled backslash escapes, or miss that unused arguments are appended as "ARGUMENTS: <value>".
---

# Skill arguments

A user passes arguments after the command: `/deploy-app staging "eu west" --dry-run`.
A skill body is a template, so each placeholder is filled in before the model reads
the skill. The backslashes in this file are escapes; Claude sees the bare form.

## What each placeholder becomes

Invocation used for every row: `/deploy-app staging "eu west" --dry-run`

| Write | Becomes |
| --- | --- |
| `\$ARGUMENTS` | `staging "eu west" --dry-run` - everything, as typed |
| `\$ARGUMENTS[0]` | `staging` - 0-based, so the first argument |
| `\$0` | `staging` - shorthand for `\$ARGUMENTS[0]` |
| `\$1` | `eu west` - shell-style quoting, so the quotes are removed |
| `\$2` | `--dry-run` |
| `\$3` | `$3` unchanged - no argument was given at that position |
| `\$env` | `staging` - only if frontmatter declares `arguments: [env, region]` |
| `\$region` | `eu west` - same declaration; an empty string if the user gave no second argument |

Named placeholders need the frontmatter declaration. The list can also be written
space-separated (`arguments: env region`).

```yaml
arguments: [env, region]
```

If no placeholder in the body receives an argument, the whole argument string is
appended to the end of the skill as `ARGUMENTS: <value>`. A skill with no
placeholders therefore still sees what the user typed.

## Escaping

- Put one backslash directly before the dollar sign to keep it literal. `\$ARGUMENTS`
  reaches the model as `$ARGUMENTS`. This works in running text, code spans and fences.
- A doubled backslash does not escape: `\\$ARGUMENTS` still expands.
- Plain `$VAR` shell variables are not substituted; only the argument forms above are.
- Built-in `${...}` variables cannot be escaped. A backslash before one is kept and the
  variable is still substituted, so leave them out of examples unless you mean them.

## Writing a skill that takes arguments

- Set `argument-hint` in frontmatter, for example `argument-hint: "[env] [region]"`,
  so the user sees what to type.
- Prefer named placeholders past one argument; `\$0` and `\$1` are harder to read.
- Describe an argument's meaning in the body, not just its placeholder, so the model
  can handle a missing or odd value.

file_path: skills/skill-args-guide/SKILL.md
content:
---
name: skill-args-guide
description: Explains how arguments passed to a skill are substituted into its SKILL.md. Covers $ARGUMENTS, $ARGUMENTS[N], and the $N shorthand, with what each becomes for a sample invocation. Use when writing or debugging a skill that takes arguments.
---

# Skill arguments guide

When a user runs a skill and types text after its name, that text is the skill's **arguments**. Claude Code substitutes the arguments into the skill body wherever a placeholder appears, before Claude reads the instructions.

## Placeholders

| Placeholder | Becomes |
|---|---|
| `$ARGUMENTS` | The entire argument string, exactly as typed |
| `$ARGUMENTS[N]` | The argument at index `N` (0-based) |
| `$N` | Shorthand for `$ARGUMENTS[N]`, e.g. `$0`, `$1`, `$2` |

Indexes start at **0**, so `$0` is the first argument, not the second.

Arguments split on whitespace. Wrap a value in double quotes to keep spaces inside one argument, and the quotes are removed.

## Worked example

Skill: `skills/fix-issue/SKILL.md`, invoked as:

```
/my-plugin:fix-issue 123 high "login page"
```

Inside the skill body:

| Placeholder | Substituted value |
|---|---|
| `$ARGUMENTS` | `123 high "login page"` |
| `$ARGUMENTS[0]` / `$0` | `123` |
| `$ARGUMENTS[1]` / `$1` | `high` |
| `$ARGUMENTS[2]` / `$2` | `login page` |
| `$3` | *(empty; no fourth argument was given)* |

So a skill body like this:

```markdown
Fix GitHub issue #$0 at priority $1.
Scope: $2.
Raw input: $ARGUMENTS
```

is read by Claude as:

```markdown
Fix GitHub issue #123 at priority high.
Scope: login page.
Raw input: 123 high "login page"
```

## Choosing a placeholder

- Use `$ARGUMENTS` when the whole input is one free-form request, such as a question or a description.
- Use `$0`, `$1`, … when the skill expects structured input and each position has a meaning.
- Use `$ARGUMENTS` alone if you want the raw string and don't need to split it.

## Gotchas

- **Missing arguments become empty.** A placeholder with no matching argument is replaced with an empty string. Write instructions that still make sense when a value is blank, or tell Claude what to do if it is.
- **Placeholders are replaced everywhere**, including inside code fences and examples in the skill body. Escape or rephrase any literal `$` text you don't want substituted.
- **Quote values that contain spaces.** Without quotes, `login page` becomes two arguments, `$1` = `login` and `$2` = `page`.
- **Skill names are namespaced in plugins.** Invoke as `/<plugin-name>:<skill-name>`, here `/my-plugin:skill-args-guide`.

---

# API error responses

Every error response from the HTTP API is an RFC 9457 problem document,
served with `Content-Type: application/problem+json`.

## Shape

```json
{
  "type": "https://errors.acme.dev/<code>",
  "title": "Short summary of this error type",
  "status": 404,
  "detail": "Plain-language explanation of this occurrence"
}
```

- `type` - always the registry URL `https://errors.acme.dev/<code>`. Never
  `about:blank`, never omitted.
- `title` - fixed per code, identical for every occurrence. Do not put
  request values in it.
- `status` - the HTTP status, repeated in the body.
- `detail` - this occurrence, in plain language. Never a stack trace, SQL,
  query text, file path or internal class name. Do not pass raw exception
  messages through; map them to a message the client can act on.

## Validation failures

Validation failures return **422**, not 400. The body carries the four
fields plus an `errors` array of `{field, message}`:

```json
{
  "type": "https://errors.acme.dev/<code>",
  "title": "Validation failed",
  "status": 422,
  "detail": "2 fields are invalid",
  "errors": [
    { "field": "email", "message": "must be a valid email address" },
    { "field": "age", "message": "must be at least 18" }
  ]
}
```

Use the code `docs/errors.md` registers for validation failures; do not
invent a new one for each endpoint.

## Adding a new error code

Every code is documented in `docs/errors.md`. Before creating a code, check
that file for one that fits. If none fits:

1. Add the code to `docs/errors.md` with its type URL, title, status and
   when it is returned.
2. Use that exact URL as `type` in the handler.

Do not ship a handler that returns a `type` with no entry in `docs/errors.md`.

## Existing ad-hoc bodies

A body like `{"error": "..."}` is not this format. When a change touches a
handler that returns one, convert the error paths in that handler to
problem+json in the same change.

content:
---
name: api-errors
description: Use when writing or changing HTTP API error responses, error handlers, validation failures, or new error codes. Enforces RFC 9457 problem+json bodies with registry type URLs, 422 for validation, and safe detail text. Trigger on "error response", "problem+json", "validation error", "422", "400", "error handler", "new error code", or any handler returning an ad-hoc {error: "..."} body.
---

# API error responses

Every error response from our HTTP API is an RFC 9457 problem details document. Do not return ad-hoc bodies such as `{"error": "..."}`. If you touch a handler that still does this, convert it.

## Response shape

Send `Content-Type: application/problem+json`. The body has these members:

| Member   | Required | Rule |
|----------|----------|------|
| `type`   | yes | A URL in the registry: `https://errors.acme.dev/<code>`. |
| `title`  | yes | A short, human-readable summary of the problem type. It does not change from one occurrence to the next. |
| `status` | yes | The HTTP status code, as a number, matching the response status line. |
| `detail` | yes | A human-readable explanation of this occurrence. See the rules below. |
| `errors` | validation only | An array of `{"field": "...", "message": "..."}` objects. |

Example, a validation failure:

```json
{
  "type": "https://errors.acme.dev/validation-failed",
  "title": "Validation failed",
  "status": 422,
  "detail": "One or more fields are invalid.",
  "errors": [
    { "field": "email", "message": "must be a valid email address" },
    { "field": "quantity", "message": "must be greater than 0" }
  ]
}
```

The `validation-failed` code above is an illustration. Use the code that `docs/errors.md` defines, or add a new one as described below.

## Status codes

- **Validation failures return 422, not 400.** This covers any request that parses but fails field validation. Include the `errors` array.
- Other error statuses are chosen for the situation as usual. They still use the same problem+json shape.

## Writing `detail`

`detail` is shown to API consumers and logged, so it must be safe to expose.

- Never include stack traces, file paths from the server, or exception dumps.
- Never include SQL, query fragments, table or column names, or driver error messages.
- Keep it to one or two plain sentences that describe what went wrong for this request.
- Do not echo back secrets or sensitive input values.

Log the full internal error server-side. Return only the sanitized `detail` to the client.

## Error codes and the registry

- Each `type` points at `https://errors.acme.dev/<code>`, where `<code>` is a stable, lowercase, hyphenated identifier.
- Every new code must be added to `docs/errors.md` in the same change that introduces it. Include the code, its `title`, the status it uses, and when it occurs.
- Do not reuse a code for a different meaning. If the meaning changes, add a new code.
- Look in `docs/errors.md` for an existing code before creating one.

## Checklist for error-handling changes

1. The response is problem+json, with `type`, `title`, `status`, and `detail`.
2. Validation failures use 422 and include an `errors` array of `{field, message}`.
3. `detail` contains no stack trace, SQL, or internal detail.
4. Any new `type` code is documented in `docs/errors.md`.
5. No handler still returns `{"error": "..."}`.

description: Writes and reviews our Postgres schema migrations against the migration safety rules. Load this before writing, reviewing, debugging or advising on any migration, even a one-line one. Without it, Claude omits lock_timeout, adds a column with a DEFAULT and NOT NULL in one statement on a large table, creates indexes without CONCURRENTLY or inside a transaction, runs backfills as one unbatched UPDATE or in the same migration as the schema change, and writes no down step or one that does not reverse the up.
---

# Migration safety

These rules apply to every Postgres migration in this repo. A migration that
breaks one is not done, even if it passes tests. Earlier Claude-written
migrations broke every rule below, so check each one explicitly; do not assume
the pattern is right because the file looks like the others.

## The rules

1. **`lock_timeout = '5s'` at the top of every migration.** First statement in
   the file, before any DDL or DML:

   ```sql
   SET lock_timeout = '5s';

   and blocks all traffic to the table while it waits.

2. **Never add a column with a DEFAULT and NOT NULL in one statement on a

1	# Skill body grammar - exact syntax
2	
3	The literal, copyable syntax behind the "Body grammar" section of
4	[SKILL.md](../SKILL.md), which holds the judgement (when to inject, why a
5	fallback, what to bound). The literals live here because a SKILL.md body is
6	preprocessed at load and a reference file, read on demand, never is.
7	
8	> Behaviour marked "observed" was seen by loading probe skills headless on
9	> Claude Code 2.1.295. Everything else is from the skills docs
10	> (https://code.claude.com/docs/en/skills, checked 2026-10-09), which now
11	> document most of what used to be observation only.
12	
13	## Where the grammar applies
14	
15	| File | Preprocessed? |
16	| --- | --- |
17	| `SKILL.md` body (and `.claude/commands/*.md`) | Yes - directives run, placeholders substitute |
18	| A skill's `references/` and other supporting files | No - plain text when Read |
19	| Subagent bodies in `.claude/agents/` or `~/.claude/agents/` | No - arrives as literal text (observed) |
20	| Subagent bodies in a plugin's `agents/` | Only the plugin path variables expand (which: the plugin-agent note in `claude-lint fields agent`); directives and argument placeholders stay literal (observed) |
21	| Rule files and CLAUDE.md | No - arrives as literal text |
22	| A skill synced from claude.ai, run on your machine | Directives never run; `@` references and some variables stay literal |
23	
24	## Dynamic context injection
25	
26	The command runs locally before the model sees the skill; its output replaces
27	the directive. Substitution is one pass over the original file: output is
28	inserted as plain text and is not re-scanned, so a command cannot emit a
29	directive for a later pass.
30	
31	Inline - an exclamation mark immediately followed by a backtick-quoted command.
32	It is recognised only at the start of a line or straight after whitespace; glued
33	to another character, as in ``KEY=!`cmd` ``, it is left as text and does not
34	run:
35	
36	```text
37	Current branch: !`git branch --show-current 2>/dev/null || echo "no data: not a git repository"`
38	```
39	
40	Fenced, for multi-line - a code fence whose opening line is three backticks
41	followed by an exclamation mark:
42	
43	````text
44	```!
45	git status --short 2>/dev/null | head -30 | grep . || echo "no data: clean tree or not a git repository"
46	git log --oneline -5 2>/dev/null || echo "no data: no commits yet"
47	```
48	````
49	
50	### The fallback pattern
51	
52	A command that exits non-zero aborts the whole skill invocation, not just its
53	own directive: Claude never sees the body, and the user gets

content:
---
description: Writes and reviews our Postgres schema migrations against the migration safety rules. Load this before writing, reviewing, debugging or advising on any migration, even a one-line one. Without it, Claude omits lock_timeout, adds a column with a DEFAULT and NOT NULL in one statement on a large table, creates indexes without CONCURRENTLY or inside a transaction, runs backfills as one unbatched UPDATE or in the same migration as the schema change, and writes no down step or one that does not reverse the up.
---

# Migration safety

These rules apply to every Postgres migration in this repo. A migration that
breaks one is not done, even if it passes tests. Earlier Claude-written
migrations broke every rule below, so check each one explicitly; do not assume
the pattern is right because the file looks like the others.

## The rules

1. **`lock_timeout = '5s'` at the top of every migration.** First statement in
   the file, before any DDL or DML:

   ```sql
   SET lock_timeout = '5s';
   ```

   Without it, a migration waiting on a lock queues behind long transactions
   and blocks all traffic to the table while it waits.

2. **Never add a column with a DEFAULT and NOT NULL in one statement on a
   large table.** Split it across migrations:

   - Migration A: `ALTER TABLE t ADD COLUMN c type;` (nullable, no default).
   - Migration B: backfill `c` in batches (rule 4).
   - Migration C: enforce the constraint without a long table scan under lock:
     `ALTER TABLE t ADD CONSTRAINT t_c_not_null CHECK (c IS NOT NULL) NOT VALID;`
     then `ALTER TABLE t VALIDATE CONSTRAINT t_c_not_null;`, then
     `ALTER TABLE t ALTER COLUMN c SET NOT NULL;`, then drop the check
     constraint.
   - Set any DEFAULT for new rows as its own step, after the backfill.

   "Large" means any table where a full rewrite or scan under lock would hurt.
   If you cannot tell the table size, treat it as large.

3. **Indexes: `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY`, outside a transaction.** Put it in
   its own migration file, marked non-transactional for the migration tool in
   use. A transaction wrapper makes `CONCURRENTLY` fail. The same applies to
   `DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY`. After a failed concurrent build, check for an
   `INVALID` index (`pg_index.indisvalid = false`) and drop it before retrying.

4. **Backfills: batches of 10k rows, in a separate migration.** Never backfill
   in the same migration as the schema change, and never run one unbatched
   `UPDATE` over the whole table. Each batch is its own statement and commits
   on its own:

   ```sql
   UPDATE orders SET status_v2 = 'pending'
   WHERE id IN (
     SELECT id FROM orders
     WHERE status_v2 IS NULL
     ORDER BY id
     LIMIT 10000
   );
   ```

   Repeat until it updates zero rows. A `DO` block runs as one transaction, so
   looping inside it does not give you committed batches; loop in the migration
   runner or a script that commits each batch.

5. **Every migration has a working down step.** The down reverses the up and
   has been run: up, then down, then up again on a copy of the schema. If a
   down cannot be fully reversible (for example, it drops a column holding
   data), write it anyway, state the data loss in a comment at the top of the
   file, and tell the user.

## Writing a migration

1. Identify the tables touched and whether any is large. If unknown, assume
   large.
2. Split the change along rules 2 and 4 before writing SQL. One concern per
   migration file.
3. Write the up with `SET lock_timeout = '5s';` first, then the DDL. Put any
   `CONCURRENTLY` index in its own file.
4. Write the down step.
5. Run the checklist below against the files you wrote.

## Reviewing a migration

Go through every file and report each violation with the file and line.
Do not report only the first one you find.

- [ ] `SET lock_timeout = '5s';` is the first statement.
- [ ] No `ADD COLUMN` combining DEFAULT and NOT NULL on a large table.
- [ ] No `CREATE INDEX` or `DROP INDEX` without `CONCURRENTLY` where the
      table is large, and no `CONCURRENTLY` inside a transaction.
- [ ] No backfill `UPDATE` in a schema migration, and no unbatched backfill.
- [ ] A down step exists, reverses the up, and states any data loss.

If a change cannot meet a rule (for example, a required NOT NULL on a table
that cannot be split), stop and say which rule and why. Do not silently break
it, and do not invent an exception.

## Scope

These rules are about safety on production Postgres. This skill does not
cover application code, query tuning, or migration tool setup, except where
the tool's transaction behaviour affects rule 3.

---
name: migration-safety
description: Write or review Postgres schema migrations against our safety rules — lock_timeout, no NOT NULL column with a default in one statement on large tables, CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY outside a transaction, batched backfills in their own migration, and a working down step. Use when creating, editing, or reviewing any migration file, or when asked whether a migration is safe to deploy.
---

# Migration safety

Our production Postgres runs migrations against live traffic. Each rule below
exists because an unsafe migration has blocked writes, held locks for minutes,
or left a database that could not be rolled back. Earlier migrations written
with Claude broke these rules, so check every rule on every migration, including
ones that look trivial.

## The rules

### 1. Start every migration with `lock_timeout`

```sql
SET lock_timeout = '5s';
```

This goes at the top of every migration, before any DDL. Without it, an `ALTER`
that waits for a lock queues behind long-running queries and blocks every query
that arrives after it. With it, the statement fails fast and the migration can
be retried.

If the migration fails with `canceling statement due to lock timeout`, retry it
later during lower traffic. Do not raise the timeout to make it pass.

### 2. Never add a NOT NULL column with a default in one statement on a large table

Do not write this on a large table:

```sql
ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN status text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'pending';  -- unsafe
```

Use this sequence instead, split across migrations:

1. **Migration A (schema):** add the column nullable with no default.
   ```sql
   ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN status text;
   ```
2. **Migration B (backfill):** fill existing rows in batches. See rule 4.
3. **Migration C (constraint):** make the column required without a long
   table scan under lock.
   ```sql
   ALTER TABLE orders ADD CONSTRAINT orders_status_not_null
     CHECK (status IS NOT NULL) NOT VALID;
   ALTER TABLE orders VALIDATE CONSTRAINT orders_status_not_null;
   ALTER TABLE orders ALTER COLUMN status SET NOT NULL;
   ALTER TABLE orders DROP CONSTRAINT orders_status_not_null;
   ```
   `VALIDATE` takes a lighter lock than a full table rewrite, and Postgres 12+
   can skip its scan for `SET NOT NULL` when a validated check constraint
   already proves the column has no nulls.
4. If new rows also need the value, set the default in a separate statement
   after the backfill: `ALTER TABLE orders ALTER COLUMN status SET DEFAULT 'pending';`

If you cannot tell whether a table is large, treat it as large.

### 3. Create indexes with `CONCURRENTLY`, outside a transaction

```sql
-- migration file contains only this statement, no BEGIN/COMMIT
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY IF NOT EXISTS orders_status_idx ON orders (status);
```

  with a loop in a procedure that `COMMIT`s per batch (`CALL` outside an

  unbatched `UPDATE` across the whole table in one transaction.
- The backfill must be safe to run more than once. Its `WHERE` clause should
  select only rows that still need work.

- Write the `down` step at the same time as the `up` step. Do not leave it empty

# Python packaging and running

uv is the only tool for Python here. Every Python task goes through it.

## Rules

- **Dependencies:** `uv add <pkg>` to add, `uv add --dev <pkg>` for dev-only,
  `uv remove <pkg>` to remove. These update `pyproject.toml` and `uv.lock` together.
- **Running code:** `uv run <command>` inside a project (for example
  `uv run pytest` or `uv run python -m mypackage`). It syncs the environment first.
- **Installing the environment:** `uv sync`. Use `uv sync --locked` in CI, so a
  stale lock fails the build instead of being silently updated.
- **Single-file scripts:** declare dependencies in a PEP 723 block at the top of
  the file, then run with `uv run script.py`. Do not create a project around it.

  ```python
  # /// script
  # requires-python = ">=3.12"
  # dependencies = [
  #   "requests<3",
  # ]
  # ///
  ```

  To add a dependency to a script, use `uv add --script script.py requests`
  rather than editing the block by hand.
- **Lock file:** `uv.lock` is committed. Never delete it to "fix" resolution
  problems; run `uv lock` and commit the result.
- **Packaging:** the project's metadata and build backend live in `pyproject.toml`.
  Build distributions with `uv build`.

## Never

- `pip install`, `pip freeze`, `python -m pip`, or `uv pip install`. The last one
  bypasses the lock file.
- `pip-tools`, `poetry`, `pipenv`, `conda`, or any other environment manager.
- Creating or activating a venv by hand: no `python -m venv`, no
  `source .venv/bin/activate`. uv manages `.venv`; use `uv run`.
- Creating `requirements.txt` or `requirements-dev.txt`, or suggesting them
  as the way to install. If a tool outside the repo insists on one, ask the user
  before generating it.
- Editing dependency lists in `pyproject.toml` or `uv.lock` by hand instead of
  using the uv commands above.

## When the user asks to "just pip install" something

Give the uv equivalent: `uv add <pkg>` in a project, or add the PEP 723 block and
`uv run script.py` for a single script. Do not offer pip as a fallback.

**uv is the only Python tool in our repos.** Do not use pip, pip-tools, poetry, or a hand-made virtualenv.

## Commands

| Task | Use | Never |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Add a dependency | `uv add <pkg>` (`uv add --dev <pkg>` for dev tools) | `pip install <pkg>`, editing requirements.txt |
| Remove a dependency | `uv remove <pkg>` | `pip uninstall`, hand-editing pyproject.toml deps then leaving the lock stale |

| Check the lock is current | `uv lock --check` (CI) | assuming the lock is fine |
| Run a single-file script | `uv run script.py` | `pip install` for its imports, then `python script.py` |

`uv run` and `uv sync` create or update `.venv` themselves. Do not create, activate, or hand-manage a virtualenv.

## Single-file scripts (PEP 723)

Scripts that are one file declare their dependencies inline. Do not create a project, pyproject.toml, or requirements file for them.

Add dependencies with uv so the metadata block is written for you:

```bash
uv add --script script.py requests rich
```

This produces a block like:

```python
# /// script
# requires-python = ">=3.12"
# dependencies = [
#   "requests",
#   "rich",
# ]
# ///
```

Run it with:

```bash
uv run script.py
```

Edit the `dependencies` list in that block by hand only if `uv add --script` is unavailable; keep it valid TOML inside the `# /// script` markers.

## Projects

- Every project has `pyproject.toml` and a committed `uv.lock`. **Commit `uv.lock`.** Changes to dependencies always come with the matching lock update in the same commit.
- Create a new project with `uv init` (add `--lib` for a library, `--package` for a package with a build backend), then `uv add` its dependencies.
- Dependencies for tests, linting, and type checking go in the dev group: `uv add --dev pytest ruff`.
- Tests and tools run through `uv run`, not from an activated environment.
- Build and publish with uv's own commands (`uv build`, `uv publish`) and the build backend declared in pyproject.toml. Do not add setup.py, setup.cfg, or a requirements.txt.

## Do not

- Write `requirements.txt`, `requirements-dev.txt`, or `constraints.txt`. The lock replaces them.
- Run `pip install`, `pip freeze`, `pip-compile`, `poetry`, or `python -m venv`.
- Use `uv pip install` or `uv pip compile`. They bypass `uv.lock`; use `uv add` and `uv sync`.
- Commit a `.venv` directory.
- Suggest any of the above as a "quick" alternative. If a tool insists on a requirements file, raise it with the user first rather than generating one.

## When you are unsure

If a task seems to need something outside this list, such as a dependency that is not on PyPI or a tool that needs a requirements file, stop and ask the user how to proceed.

argument-hint: "[since-tag or version]"

Draft release notes for changes merged since the previous release.

Range: $ARGUMENTS
If no argument is given, use the most recent tag (`git describe --tags --abbrev=0`). If there are no tags, stop and ask which starting point to use.

## Gather

1. List merged PRs since the starting point, with number, title, author, labels and URL, e.g. `gh pr list --state merged --limit 200 --json number,title,author,labels,url,mergedAt`. Keep only those merged after the starting point.
2. For each PR whose title or labels are ambiguous, run `gh pr view <number> --json files,body` to see which files it touched.

## Filter

Leave out, and list them in a separate "Excluded" section so the user can check the call:

- Dependency bumps: Dependabot or Renovate authors, "bump" or "chore(deps)" titles, or changes only to lockfiles and manifests with no behaviour change.
- CI-only PRs: changes only under `.github/`, CI config, or build scripts with no effect on the shipped plugin.

Do not drop a PR for being small. A one-line fix that changes behaviour stays in.

## Classify

- **BREAKING**: anything that requires users to change how they call, configure or install the plugin. Each gets a one-line migration note saying what to do instead.
- **Added**: new skills, commands, agents, hooks or options.
- **Changed**: behaviour changes that are not breaking, and refactors users can see.
- **Fixed**: bug fixes.

Group by the change, not the author. Never write author names or handles as headings or group labels.

## Format

Use this order and omit any empty section:

```
## BREAKING
- <what changed> - Migration: <one line>. ([#123](<PR url>))

## Added
- <entry> ([#123](<PR url>))

## Changed
- <entry> ([#124](<PR url>))

## Fixed
- <entry> ([#125](<PR url>))
```

Every entry links its PR number. Write each entry as one short line describing the user-visible effect, not the implementation. Keep the PR title's meaning; do not copy it verbatim if it is unclear.

End with an "Excluded" list: PR number, title, and the reason (dependency bump or CI-only).

Print the draft in the conversation. Do not write it to a file or publish it unless the user asks.

---

# Release notes

Draft release notes from the PRs merged since the last release. The draft goes to the user for review; do not publish it, create a release, or edit CHANGELOG files unless the user asks.

## House rules (always apply)

1. **Group by change type, never by PR author.** Only three headings, in this order: `### Added`, `### Changed`, `### Fixed`. Do not write author names or "thanks to @x" groupings.
2. **Leave out dependency bumps and CI-only PRs.** Skip a PR if it is a dependency update (Dependabot/Renovate authors, titles like "bump", "update dependency", "chore(deps)", lockfile-only changes) or if every changed file is CI/tooling config (`.github/`, CI pipeline files, workflow-only changes). If a PR mixes a real user-facing change with a dependency bump, keep the user-facing change and drop the bump.
3. **Every entry links its PR number**, in the form `(#123)` pointing at the PR. No entry without a number.
4. **Breaking changes go first** under a `### BREAKING` heading, above Added/Changed/Fixed. Each breaking entry gets a one-line migration note, e.g. `Migration: rename \`--out\` to \`--output\`.` A breaking change that also appears in Changed should be listed only under BREAKING.

## Steps

1. **Find the range.** Use the latest tag as the base: `git describe --tags --abbrev=0`. If there are no tags, ask the user for the starting ref. The target is `HEAD` unless the user names another.
2. **List merged PRs in the range.** Prefer `gh pr list --state merged --base main --search "merged:>=<tag date>"` or `gh api` against the merge commits. Fall back to `git log <base>..HEAD --merges` and parse PR numbers from merge subjects (`Merge pull request #N`) or squash subjects (`... (#N)`). Use the PR title and body, not just the commit subject, to understand the change.
3. **Filter.** Apply rule 2. Note every PR you dropped and why, so the user can overrule you.
4. **Classify each remaining PR** as Added (new capability), Changed (behavior or API change that is not a bug fix), Fixed (bug fix), or BREAKING (removes or alters existing behavior in a way users must act on). When unsure, say so in the notes for the user rather than guessing.
5. **Write the entries.** One line per PR, written from the user's point of view, starting with a verb or noun phrase, ending with the PR link. Keep each entry short; merge several PRs into one entry only when they are the same change.
6. **Check before returning.** Confirm: no author-based grouping; no dependency or CI-only entries; every entry has a PR number; BREAKING comes first and each has a migration line; headings are only Added/Changed/Fixed (plus BREAKING).

## Output format

```markdown
## vX.Y.Z — YYYY-MM-DD

### BREAKING
- Removed `legacy_mode` option (#412)
  Migration: set `mode = "standard"` instead of `legacy_mode = true`.

### Added

graders.evidence:
---
description: Use when writing, reviewing, debugging or advising on Textual TUI code in our apps (we are on Textual 8), before editing widgets, screens, apps or queries, even a small change. Claude's recall is mostly pre-1.0 and gets Textual 8 wrong: Static.renderable is now Static.content, Select.BLANK is now Select.NULL, App.query searches the default screen not the active one, and optional lookups use query_one_optional rather than catching NoMatches.
---

# Textual 8

Our apps target Textual 8. Code written from memory tends to use pre-1.0
names that no longer exist or behave differently. Use the names below, and
check anything else against the installed package before relying on it.

## Renamed or changed APIs

- **`Static.renderable` is now `Static.content`.** Read and set `content`.
- **`Select.BLANK` is now `Select.NULL`.**
- **Query from the screen, not the app.** `App.query` searches the default
  screen, not the one that is active. Inside a screen or widget, use
  `self.query_one(...)` or `self.query(...)`. From the app, go through the
  active screen: `self.screen.query_one(...)`.
- **Optional lookup uses `query_one_optional`.** It returns `None` when the
  widget is absent. Do not wrap `query_one` in `try`/`except NoMatches`.

## Before relying on any other Textual name

- Confirm the name exists in the installed Textual 8, for example with
  `python -c "import textual; print(textual.__version__)"` and by grepping the
  package source for the class or method.

---
name: textual-8
description: Write or edit Textual TUI code for Textual 8. Use when creating or changing Textual apps, screens, widgets, CSS, bindings, messages, workers, or Textual tests. Corrects pre-1.0 API habits (Static.renderable, Select.BLANK, App-level query, catching NoMatches).
---

# Textual 8

Target **Textual 8**. Much of what is remembered about Textual predates 1.0 and no longer works. Do not write from memory. Use the APIs below, and when unsure, check the installed package (`python -c "import textual; print(textual.__file__)"`) or the docs for the pinned version.

## Renamed or changed APIs

| Old (pre-1.0 habit) | Textual 8 |
| --- | --- |
| `Static.renderable` | `Static.content` (read and set) |
| `Select.BLANK` | `Select.NULL` |
| `self.app.query(...)` to find widgets on the current screen | `self.query(...)` from the screen or widget that owns them |
| `try: self.query_one(...) except NoMatches:` | `self.query_one_optional(...)` returns the widget or `None` |

```python
# Wrong
self.query_one("#status", Static).renderable = "Ready"
select.value = Select.BLANK
self.app.query_one("#name", Input)          # searches the default screen
try:
    btn = self.query_one("#save", Button)
except NoMatches:
    btn = None

# Right
self.query_one("#status", Static).content = "Ready"
select.value = Select.NULL
self.screen.query_one("#name", Input)      # or self.query_one(...) inside the screen
btn = self.query_one_optional("#save", Button)
```

file_path: skills/textual-8/SKILL.md
content:
---
name: textual-8
description: Write or edit Textual TUI code for Textual 8. Use when creating or changing Textual apps, screens, widgets, CSS, bindings, messages, workers, or Textual tests. Corrects pre-1.0 API habits (Static.renderable, Select.BLANK, App-level query, catching NoMatches).
---

# Textual 8

Target **Textual 8**. Much of what is remembered about Textual predates 1.0 and no longer works. Do not write from memory. Use the APIs below, and when unsure, check the installed package (`python -c "import textual; print(textual.__file__)"`) or the docs for the pinned version.

## Renamed or changed APIs

| Old (pre-1.0 habit) | Textual 8 |
| --- | --- |
| `Static.renderable` | `Static.content` (read and set) |
| `Select.BLANK` | `Select.NULL` |
| `self.app.query(...)` to find widgets on the current screen | `self.query(...)` from the screen or widget that owns them |
| `try: self.query_one(...) except NoMatches:` | `self.query_one_optional(...)` returns the widget or `None` |

```python
# Wrong
self.query_one("#status", Static).renderable = "Ready"
select.value = Select.BLANK
self.app.query_one("#name", Input)          # searches the default screen
try:
    btn = self.query_one("#save", Button)
except NoMatches:
    btn = None

# Right
self.query_one("#status", Static).content = "Ready"
select.value = Select.NULL
self.screen.query_one("#name", Input)      # or self.query_one(...) inside the screen
btn = self.query_one_optional("#save", Button)
```

`App.query` searches the default screen, not the active one. If a modal or pushed screen holds the widget, query that screen (`self.screen` or a reference to it). Do not query through `self.app`.

## App and screen structure

- Build the UI in `compose()` with `yield`. Mount children from there, not in `__init__`.
- Use `CSS_PATH` for a stylesheet file or `CSS` for an inline string. Keep layout and colour in CSS, not in Python.
- Use `ModalScreen` for dialogs. Pass results back with `self.dismiss(result)` and handle them in the `push_screen` callback, or with `await self.app.push_screen_wait(...)` inside a worker.
- Declare keys with `BINDINGS = [Binding("ctrl+s", "save", "Save")]`. Each binding calls the `action_<name>` method.

```python
from textual.app import App, ComposeResult
from textual.binding import Binding
from textual.widgets import Button, Footer, Header, Static


class DemoApp(App):
    CSS_PATH = "demo.tcss"
    BINDINGS = [Binding("q", "quit", "Quit")]

    def compose(self) -> ComposeResult:
        yield Header()
        yield Static("Idle", id="status")
        yield Button("Start", id="start", variant="primary")
        yield Footer()

    def on_button_pressed(self, event: Button.Pressed) -> None:
        if event.button.id == "start":
            self.query_one("#status", Static).content = "Running"
```

## Events and messages

- Handle messages with `on_<message_name>` methods or `@on(Button.Pressed, "#start")`. The decorator is clearer when several widgets share a handler.
- Custom messages subclass `Message` and are sent with `self.post_message(...)`. Put them on the widget that owns the state, nested inside it, e.g. `class Panel.Changed(Message)`.
- Use `reactive` attributes for state that should redraw the UI. Set the value and let the watcher or `compute_*` method react, rather than calling `refresh()` by hand.

## Background work

- Do not block the event loop. Slow I/O or CPU work goes in a worker: `@work(exclusive=True)` on a method, or `self.run_worker(fn, thread=True)`.
- From a thread worker, update the UI with `self.app.call_from_thread(...)`. Do not touch widgets from another thread directly.
- Cancel and clean up in `on_unmount`, or rely on workers being tied to their node.

## Tables, inputs, and selects

- `DataTable`: call `add_columns(...)` once, then `add_row(...)`. Pass `key=` to `add_row` if you need to find the row later.
- `Input` posts `Input.Submitted` on enter and `Input.Changed` on edit.
- `Select` posts `Select.Changed`. Use `Select.NULL` for "nothing selected". Do not use `Select.BLANK`.

## Testing

Use `app.run_test()` with the Pilot object. Do not drive a real terminal.

```python
import pytest
from demo import DemoApp
from textual.widgets import Static


@pytest.mark.asyncio
async def test_start_sets_status():
    async with DemoApp().run_test() as pilot:
        await pilot.click("#start")
        await pilot.pause()
        assert pilot.app.screen.query_one("#status", Static).content == "Running"
```

Query the screen in tests, the same as in app code. Use `pilot.press(...)` for key bindings. Use `pilot.pause()` after actions that schedule UI updates.

## Checklist before finishing

- No `.renderable`, `Select.BLANK`, `app.query`, or `except NoMatches` in the diff.
- Widgets on a pushed or modal screen are queried from that screen.
- Missing optional widgets use `query_one_optional`.
- Slow work runs in a worker, and UI updates from threads go through `call_from_thread`.
- Styling lives in CSS.

Current DEPLOY_ENV value (read when this skill loaded):

!`printf 'DEPLOY_ENV=%s\n' "${DEPLOY_ENV:-<unset>}"`

Do the following:

   - `dev` / `development` / `local`: developer sandbox for building and testing; data and uptime are not guaranteed.
   - `test` / `qa` / `ci`: automated or manual testing environment, typically reset between runs.
   - Any other value: say it is not one of the conventional names, and describe it only as far as the project's own config or docs establish. Do not guess.
3. If the project defines what its environments do (for example in a README, deploy config, or docs), prefer that description over the generic one above and say where it came from.

model | haiku|sonnet|opus|fable|inherit or a full model id | the session model | model for the rest of the current turn (the session model resumes on the next prompt); with `context: fork` it...
effort | low|medium|high|xhigh|max or an integer | the session effort | effort level while the skill is active; the levels available depend on the model
context | fork|inline | inline | `fork` runs the body as the prompt of a fresh subagent, which does not inherit the conversation
agent | string | general-purpose | with `context: fork`, the subagent type that hosts the fork: `Explore`, `Plan`, `general-purpose` or a custom...
background | boolean | true | with `context: fork` only: false makes the turn wait for the fork's result. A background fork gets the... [since 2.1.218]
hooks | map | - | hooks registered when the skill is first invoked and kept until the session ends; `once: true` on a handler...
paths | YAML list or comma-separated string of globs | - | gates automatic activation to work on matching files; a manual `/name` is not gated. Same glob format as a...
shell | bash|powershell | bash | shell that runs the body's injected commands
metadata | map | - | free-form data for your own tooling; accepted, not acted on, and a value that is not a map is dropped
license | string | - | licence covering the skill (Agent Skills spec); accepted, not acted on

(effects ending in ... are cut short: python3 "/home/claude/work/authoring-kit/scripts/claude-lint" fields skill <field> prints one field in full, --full the whole table)

notes:
- An unrecognised field is ignored without an error. The docs say a name must match this table exactly; the build verified here also accepts a known name spelt with different case, hyphens or underscores.
- Frontmatter is read only when `---` is the file's first line; YAML that does not parse leaves the skill loaded with no fields set.
- Booleans also accept yes/no/on/off/1/0 in any case (2.1.218 and later).
- A `.claude/commands/` file takes the same fields except `name` and `paths`: there the file name is the command.
- claude.ai uploads, the Skills API and `package_skill.py` allow only `name`, `description`, `license`, `compatibility`, `metadata` and `allowed-tools`; any other field fails the upload with "Unexpected key(s) in SKILL.md frontmatter", and the body grammar does nothing there.
- Listing budget: `description` + `when_to_use` are cut at 1,536 characters per skill (the `skillListingMaxDescChars` setting moves the cap).
- The whole skill listing gets 1% of the context window (`skillListingBudgetFraction`); over budget, names stay while descriptions are dropped starting with the least-invoked skills.
- `allowed-tools` Bash rules: `Bash(cmd *)` and `Bash(cmd:*)` match with a wildcard, `Bash(cmd)` only the bare word; a lowercase `bash(...)` matches nothing; a quoted path must be quoted the same way in the rule and the command. `claude-lint check-injection` answers whether a given command is covered.
- In an `allowed-tools` rule the skill-dir and project-dir variables (and in a plugin skill the plugin-root and plugin-data ones) expand as they do in the body. `allowManagedPermissionRulesOnly` ignores the field for project and personal skills.
- A fork that needs the conversation history cannot get it from `context: fork`: the user forks the conversation instead (`/subtask`; `/fork` before 2.1.212).
- Also accepted by this build's schema, undocumented, and not flagged as unknown: version, disallowedTools, fallback, created_by, improved_by, mcpServers, lspServers, agents, outputStyles, themes, workflows, channels, monitors, settings, userConfig, defaultEnabled, experimental, dependencies, displayName, author, homepage, repository, keywords.
---
# Skill body grammar - exact syntax

The literal, copyable syntax behind the "Body grammar" section of
[SKILL.md](../SKILL.md), which holds the judgement (when to inject, why a
fallback, what to bound). The literals live here because a SKILL.md body is
preprocessed at load and a reference file, read on demand, never is.

> Behaviour marked "observed" was seen by loading probe skills headless on
> Claude Code 2.1.295. Everything else is from the skills docs
> (https://code.claude.com/docs/en/skills, checked 2026-10-09), which now
> document most of what used to be observation only.

trajectory.title: skills/ci-failure/SKILL.md
trajectory.body:
file_path: skills/ci-failure/SKILL.md
content:
---
description: Find the failing test in CI logs and report only its name and error. Use when a CI run failed and you need to know which test broke and why, before debugging or fixing anything. Load this instead of reading CI logs by hand: the logs are too large to read whole, and the first real failure is easy to lose among cascaded ones.
argument-hint: [log-file-or-directory]
context: fork
agent: general-purpose
background: false
effort: medium
allowed-tools: Bash(grep:*) Bash(tail:*) Bash(sed:*) Bash(ls:*) Bash(find:*) Bash(wc:*)
---

You are investigating a failed CI run. Your final message is the only thing
the user will see, so it must contain only the failing test's name and its
error. Do not paste log excerpts, stack traces, or your search process.

Log location: $ARGUMENTS
If that is empty, search the project for CI output: directories named
`ci-logs`, `logs`, `test-results` or `artifacts`, and files named `*.log`,
`*.xml` (JUnit) or `*.txt` that look like test output. Prefer the most
recently modified candidates. Do not read the whole of any file.

Method:

1. Get the size of each candidate (`wc -l`) and find failure markers with
   `grep -n`, not by reading. Useful markers across common formats:
   `FAILED`, `FAIL:`, `--- FAIL`, `✕`, `●`, `##[error]`, `<failure`,
   `<error`, `Traceback`, `AssertionError`, `Error:`.
2. Work out the first real failure. Later failures often follow from an
   earlier one (setup errors, a crashed suite, a timeout), so look at the
   earliest failing test in run order, and read only the lines around its
   marker with `sed -n 'START,ENDp'`, keeping the window small.
3. If the failing test's own error is unclear, check the lines just before
   its marker for the cause. Do not read past the end of its block.
4. Do not modify any file, and do not try to fix the test.

Report, in this exact shape and nothing else:

```
Test: <full test name, as the runner printed it>
Error: <the error message, at most three lines, with no stack trace>
```

If several tests failed, report only the first one and append a single line
`(N other failures in <log path>)`. If no failure can be found, reply with
one line saying so and naming the paths you searched. If the log location
does not exist, say that instead.

content:
---
name: ci-failure
description: Find the failing test in CI logs and report only its name and error message. Use when the user asks why CI failed, which test broke, or to triage a red build from log files. The logs are large, so the investigation runs in an isolated context and only the result is returned.
argument-hint: "[log file, log directory, or CI run URL]"
allowed-tools: Bash, Read, Grep, Glob, Agent
context: fork
---

# ci-failure

Goal: identify the first failing test in the CI logs and report exactly two things, its **name** and its **error**. Nothing else goes back to the main conversation.

## Output contract

Your final message must be only this, with no preamble and no log excerpts beyond the error:

```
Failing test: <full test name, including suite/class if the log shows it>
Error: <the error message, at most 5 lines; include the assertion or exception type and the first line of the message>
Location: <file:line if the log shows it, otherwise omit this line>
```

If more than one test failed, add one line `Other failures: <count>` and nothing more. Do not list them.

If no failing test can be found, reply `No failing test found in <source>` plus one line on what you searched. Do not guess.

## Step 0: Delegate if you are not already isolated

If this skill was not run in a forked context (you can tell because you are reading this in the main conversation with a full history), do not investigate inline. Instead call the Agent tool with `subagent_type: "general-purpose"` and a prompt that says: "Follow the ci-failure skill at `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/skills/ci-failure/SKILL.md` (or the copy in this plugin's `skills/ci-failure/`) for the source `<argument>`. Return only the output contract." Pass the user's argument through verbatim. Return that agent's result as your answer.

## Step 1: Locate the logs

Use the argument if one was given:

- **A file**: use it directly.
- **A directory**: search it with `Glob` for `*.log`, `*.txt`, `*.xml` (JUnit), `*.json`, and `*.out`, newest first.
- **A URL**: do not download blindly. Ask the user for a local copy or the `gh run view <id> --log-failed` output path. Use `gh` only if it is already authenticated and the user gave a run ID.

With no argument, look in these locations in order and use the first that exists and is non-empty: `ci-logs/`, `logs/`, `test-results/`, `test-reports/`, `build/test-results/`, `target/surefire-reports/`, `junit*.xml`, `*.log` in the repo root.

Record the file size before reading. Never `cat` a file you have not sized.

## Step 2: Find failure markers without reading the whole file

Search with `Grep` using `output_mode: "content"` and `head_limit` (start at 50). Try these patterns, case-insensitive, most specific first:

- JUnit XML: `<failure`, `<error ` (the test name is in the enclosing `<testcase name=...>`)
- Generic: `FAILED`, `FAIL:`, `--- FAIL`, `\bnot ok\b`, `✗`, `✕`
- Language markers: `AssertionError`, `Traceback \(most recent call last\)`, `panicked at`, `Exception in thread`, `Error:`

Pick the **earliest** real test failure. Later failures are often cascades from the first, and that is what the user usually wants. Confirm the match is a test failure and not a log line that merely mentions the word (for example a passing test named `error_handling`).

## Step 3: Read a small window around the match

Use `Read` with `offset` and `limit` (about 40 lines before the match, 40 after). Do not read past the end of the failure block into unrelated output. For JUnit, the `<testcase>` element is enough.

Extract:

- The full test name, including the suite or class if printed.
- The error: exception or assertion type and the first line of its message. Strip ANSI color codes and timestamps. Keep at most 5 lines.
- The `file:line` from the stack trace, only if it points into the project's own code and not into a framework or stdlib frame.

## Step 4: Count the rest

Run one `Grep` with `output_mode: "count"` for the same failure markers to fill in `Other failures`. Do not print them.

## Rules

- Never paste raw log output into the reply. Quote only the error, trimmed.
- Never modify logs, the repo, or CI config. This skill is read-only.
- Do not re-run tests. The job is to read the logs, not to reproduce.
- If the log is truncated or the failure block is missing, say so in the reply as: `Error: log appears truncated before the failure; the first failure could not be confirmed.`

1	# Skill body grammar - exact syntax
2	
3	The literal, copyable syntax behind the "Body grammar" section of
4	[SKILL.md](../SKILL.md), which holds the judgement (when to inject, why a
5	fallback, what to bound). The literals live here because a SKILL.md body is
6	preprocessed at load and a reference file, read on demand, never is.
7	
8	> Behaviour marked "observed" was seen by loading probe skills headless on
9	> Claude Code 2.1.295. Everything else is from the skills docs
10	> (https://code.claude.com/docs/en/skills, checked 2026-10-09), which now
11	> document most of what used to be observation only.
12	
13	## Where the grammar applies
14	
15	| File | Preprocessed? |
16	| --- | --- |
17	| `SKILL.md` body (and `.claude/commands/*.md`) | Yes - directives run, placeholders substitute |
18	| A skill's `references/` and other supporting files | No - plain text when Read |
19	| Subagent bodies in `.claude/agents/` or `~/.claude/agents/` | No - arrives as literal text (observed) |
20	| Subagent bodies in a plugin's `agents/` | Only the plugin path variables expand (which: the plugin-agent note in `claude-lint fields agent`); directives and argument placeholders stay literal (observed) |
21	| Rule files and CLAUDE.md | No - arrives as literal text |
22	| A skill synced from claude.ai, run on your machine | Directives never run; `@` references and some variables stay literal |
23	
24	## Dynamic context injection
25	
26	The command runs locally before the model sees the skill; its output replaces
27	the directive. Substitution is one pass over the original file: output is
28	inserted as plain text and is not re-scanned, so a command cannot emit a
29	directive for a later pass.
30	
31	Inline - an exclamation mark immediately followed by a backtick-quoted command.
32	It is recognised only at the start of a line or straight after whitespace; glued
33	to another character, as in ``KEY=!`cmd` ``, it is left as text and does not
34	run:
35	
36	```text
37	Current branch: !`git branch --show-current 2>/dev/null || echo "no data: not a git repository"`
38	```
39	
40	Fenced, for multi-line - a code fence whose opening line is three backticks
41	followed by an exclamation mark:
42	
43	````text
44	```!
45	git status --short 2>/dev/null | head -30 | grep . || echo "no data: clean tree or not a git repository"
46	git log --oneline -5 2>/dev/null || echo "no data: no commits yet"
47	```
48	````
49	
50	### The fallback pattern
51	
52	A command that exits non-zero aborts the whole skill invocation, not just its
53	own directive: Claude never sees the body, and the user gets
54	`Shell command failed for pattern "..."` with the output under `[stderr]`
55	(docs; observed with an exit code of 3). The one carve-out is exit code 1 from
56	search and comparison commands such as `grep` and `diff`, which is treated as a
57	normal result. With the default bash shell stderr is merged into the injected
58	text. Silencing it with `2>/dev/null` does not change the exit status, so that
59	alone still aborts (observed). Silence it and chain an echo so the skill
60	degrades into something actionable instead of failing to load:
61	
62	```text
63	!`cmd 2>/dev/null || echo "no data: <reason>"`
64	```
65	
66	The docs' own idiom for a command expected to exit non-zero is a trailing
67	`|| true`; the echo form is the same guard with a reason attached. `claude-lint`
68	rule SK005 flags a directive with neither.
69	
70	### Reading an environment variable
71	
72	Ordinary shell variables written in body text (`$VAR`) are not expanded. Read
73	one with `printenv`, pre-approved for that one name:
74	
75	```text
76	allowed-tools: Bash(printenv DEPLOY_ENV)
77	
78	!`printenv DEPLOY_ENV 2>/dev/null || echo "no data: DEPLOY_ENV is not set"`
79	```
80	
81	The obvious `echo $VAR` does not load: an echo that expands a variable fails the
82	permission check, quoted or not, and a `Bash(echo *)` entry does not rescue it
83	(observed; only `$HOME`, and `$USER` inside double quotes, got through without
84	blanket `Bash`).
85	
86	### Bounding the output
87	
88	The cap goes in the command itself, as a pipe into `head`. That pipe also
89	guards the exit status - a trailing `head` succeeds even when the command
90	before it failed - but for the same reason a fallback chained after it never
91	fires, and the body gets an empty result. Put `grep .` after `head` to turn
92	empty output into the fallback (it also drops blank lines). Each command also
93	runs under the Bash tool's default 2-minute timeout:
94	
95	```text
96	!`git diff --stat 2>/dev/null | head -40 | grep . || echo "no data: no diff"`
97	!`gh pr view --json title,body 2>/dev/null | head -c 4000 | grep . || echo "no data: no PR for this branch"`
98	```
99	
100	The second needs `allowed-tools: Bash(gh pr view *)`; `git diff`, `head` and
101	`grep` pass as read-only. Do not put the fallback inside the pipe by wrapping
102	it in parentheses or braces - `(cmd || echo ...) | head` fails the permission
103	check unless the skill has blanket `Bash` (all observed on 2.1.295).
104	
105	## Argument substitutions
106	
107	| Form | Substitutes |

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Group merged PR titles from a CSV by conventional-commit prefix."""

import csv
import re
import sys
from collections import defaultdict

PREFIXES = ("feat", "fix", "chore")
# Matches "type:", "type(scope):", and "type!:" / "type(scope)!:" forms.
TITLE_RE = re.compile(r"^(?P<type>[A-Za-z]+)(?:\([^)]*\))?!?:\s*\S")


def group_titles(rows, column):
    groups = defaultdict(list)
    for row in rows:
        title = (row.get(column) or "").strip()
        if not title:
            continue
        match = TITLE_RE.match(title)
        kind = match.group("type").lower() if match else None
        groups[kind if kind in PREFIXES else "other"].append(title)
    return groups


def main():
    if len(sys.argv) not in (2, 3):
        sys.exit(f"usage: {sys.argv[0]} prs.csv [title-column]")

    path = sys.argv[1]
    column = sys.argv[2] if len(sys.argv) == 3 else "title"

    with open(path, newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        reader = csv.DictReader(f)
        fieldnames = reader.fieldnames or []
        if column not in fieldnames:
            sys.exit(f"column {column!r} not found; columns are: {', '.join(fieldnames)}")
        groups = group_titles(reader, column)

    for key in (*PREFIXES, "other"):
        titles = groups.get(key, [])
        if not titles:
            continue
        print(f"{key} ({len(titles)})")
        for title in titles:
            print(f"  - {title}")
        print()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

Usage: `python3 group_prs.py prs.csv` reads the `title` column. Pass a second argument to use a different column name. Titles are matched case-insensitively, scopes and `!` breaking markers are accepted, and anything without a `feat`/`fix`/`chore` prefix goes under `other`. I haven't run this against a real file.

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Group merged PR titles from a CSV by conventional-commit prefix."""

import argparse
import csv
import re
import sys
from collections import defaultdict

PREFIXES = ("feat", "fix", "chore")
PREFIX_RE = re.compile(r"^(feat|fix|chore)(\([^)]*\))?!?:\s*", re.IGNORECASE)


def group_titles(rows, column):
    groups = defaultdict(list)
    for row in rows:
        title = (row.get(column) or "").strip()
        if not title:
            continue
        match = PREFIX_RE.match(title)
        if match:
            prefix = match.group(1).lower()
            groups[prefix].append(title[match.end():].strip() or title)
        else:
            groups["other"].append(title)
    return groups


def main():
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__)
    parser.add_argument("csv_path", help="CSV file containing PR titles")
    parser.add_argument("--column", default="title", help="Column holding the PR title (default: title)")
    args = parser.parse_args()

    try:
        with open(args.csv_path, newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
            reader = csv.DictReader(f)
            if reader.fieldnames is None or args.column not in reader.fieldnames:
                sys.exit(f"error: column '{args.column}' not found in {args.csv_path}")
            groups = group_titles(reader, args.column)
    except OSError as exc:
        sys.exit(f"error: {exc}")

    for prefix in (*PREFIXES, "other"):
        titles = groups.get(prefix, [])
        if not titles:
            continue
        print(f"{prefix} ({len(titles)})")
        for title in titles:
            print(f"  - {title}")
        print()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

The script assumes the titles are in a column named `title`; pass `--column` to use a different one. It prints each prefix group with its count, strips the prefix from each line, and puts anything without a `feat`/`fix`/`chore` prefix under `other`.

185-A plugin ships hooks in `hooks/hooks.json` at the plugin root, and may add more

file_path: hooks/db-conventions-context.sh
content:
#!/bin/sh
# PreToolUse on Edit|Write: when the target file is under src/db/, hand the
# db-conventions skill body to Claude as additional context before the edit.
# Never blocks: any failure exits 0 with no output.

skill="${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/skills/db-conventions/SKILL.md"
project="${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR:-$PWD}"

file=$(jq -r '.tool_input.file_path // empty' 2>/dev/null)
[ -n "$file" ] || exit 0

rel="${file#"$project"/}"
case "$rel" in
  src/db/*) ;;
  *) exit 0 ;;
esac

[ -r "$skill" ] || exit 0

# Strip the YAML frontmatter, keep the body.
body=$(awk 'BEGIN{n=0} /^---$/ && n<2 {n++; next} n>=2 {print}' "$skill")
[ -n "$body" ] || exit 0

jq -n --arg file "$rel" --arg body "$body" '{
  hookSpecificOutput: {
    hookEventName: "PreToolUse",
    additionalContext: ("Editing \($file): apply the database conventions below.\n\n" + $body)
  }
}'
exit 0

trajectory.body:
I added the `db-conventions` skill and a hook that loads it before any `Edit` or `Write` under `src/db/`. The conventions themselves are still placeholders, because I couldn't find them anywhere in this environment.

**Why a hook and not just the skill:** a skill's `paths` filter only offers the skill, and a plugin doesn't load `rules/`. So the skill alone can't guarantee it's loaded whenever `src/db/` is edited. The hook runs deterministically on every matching edit.

**Files:**
- `skills/db-conventions/SKILL.md`: the conventions, with `user-invocable: false` since it's background knowledge. Each rule is a marked placeholder, with a TODO to replace them.
- `hooks/hooks.json`: a `PreToolUse` hook on `Edit|Write`.
- `hooks/db-conventions-context.sh`: if the target path is under `src/db/`, it returns the skill body as `additionalContext`. Otherwise it exits 0 silently. It never blocks.

**Checks:** `hooktool validate` passes with no warnings. I ran the script by hand: a `src/db/` path returns the conventions, a non-db path and empty input produce no output. I did not run a live Claude Code session, and I did not run `claude plugin validate`.

**Limits:**
- The hook only sees `Edit` and `Write`. A change made through Bash (`sed -i`, `tee`, redirects) bypasses it.
- It fails open. If `jq` or the skill file is missing, the edit goes ahead without the conventions. Setting `onFailure: block` would make a missing script block every edit, which seemed too heavy.
- It re-injects the conventions on every matching edit, so keep the skill body short. Claude Code caps injected context at 10,000 characters.

**Needed from you:** the actual database conventions, to replace the four placeholder rules in `SKILL.md`. Once they're in, the hook delivers them automatically. I haven't committed anything.

content:
---
name: triage
description: Set the priority label on a GitHub issue using the gh CLI. Use when the user asks to triage, prioritize, or label an issue with a priority (for example "/triage 123 p1").
argument-hint: <issue-number> <priority>
disable-model-invocation: true
allowed-tools: Bash(gh issue view:*), Bash(gh issue edit:*)
---

# Triage an issue

Set the priority label on issue `$ARGUMENTS` in the current repository.

Arguments are `<issue-number> <priority>`, for example `/triage 123 p1` or `/triage 123 high`.

## Steps

1. **Parse the arguments.** The first token must be a positive integer, and the second must be a priority from the table below. If either is missing or invalid, stop and show the usage line. Do not guess.

2. **Map the priority to a label** (case-insensitive):

   | Input                 | Label         |
   |-----------------------|---------------|
   | `p0`, `critical`, `urgent` | `priority:P0` |
   | `p1`, `high`          | `priority:P1` |
   | `p2`, `medium`, `normal`   | `priority:P2` |
   | `p3`, `low`           | `priority:P3` |

3. **Read the issue's current labels:**

   ```
   gh issue view <N> --json number,title,state,labels
   ```

   If the issue does not exist, stop and report the error from `gh`.

4. **Find stale priority labels.** Any label on the issue that starts with `priority:` and is not the target label is stale. Leave every other label alone.

5. **Apply the change in one edit:**

   ```
   gh issue edit <N> --add-label "<target>" --remove-label "<stale1>,<stale2>"
   ```

   Omit `--remove-label` if there are no stale labels.

6. **Verify** by running step 3 again and confirming the issue has exactly one `priority:*` label, the target.

7. **Report** the issue number and title, the old priority (or "none"), and the new priority.

## Failure cases

- If `gh` reports that a label does not exist, stop and tell the user which label is missing. Do not create labels on your own. Offer to create it with `gh label create`.
- If `gh` reports an authentication error, stop and tell the user to run `gh auth login`.

The skill is advisory. Claude decides whether to load it based on its description, and once loaded it is still just guidance Claude may or may not follow. To make a rule hold every time, enforce it outside the model with a hook, and back it up with a check that runs for every change, including the ones Claude doesn't make.

**1. Hook for Claude's edits (deterministic)**

A `PostToolUse` hook runs after every `Edit`, `Write`, or `MultiEdit`. If it exits with code 2, its stderr goes back to Claude, which then has to fix the file. In `.claude/settings.json`:

```json
{
  "hooks": {
    "PostToolUse": [
      {
        "matcher": "Edit|Write|MultiEdit",
        "hooks": [
          { "type": "command", "command": "\"$CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR\"/.claude/hooks/check-api-validation.sh" }
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
}
```

And `.claude/hooks/check-api-validation.sh` (needs `jq`, and `chmod +x`):

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
f=$(jq -r '.tool_input.file_path // empty')
case "$f" in */src/api/*.ts) ;; *) exit 0 ;; esac
[ -f "$f" ] || exit 0
if ! grep -qE "from ['\"]zod['\"]" "$f" || ! grep -qE '\.(safe)?parse\(' "$f"; then
  echo "src/api handlers must validate the request body with a zod schema before using it (api-conventions). Add the schema and parse before touching req.body." >&2
  exit 2
fi
```

This check is a heuristic. It confirms that the file imports zod and calls `parse`, but not that the parse happens before the body is used. Adjust the path glob and the patterns to match how your handlers are actually written, and exclude any non-handler files under `src/api/`. I haven't run this against your repo.

**2. CI check (covers everything, including human edits)**

A hook only sees Claude's edits. Add the same rule as an ESLint rule or a test that fails the build when a handler lacks validation. That is the real guarantee, and it also catches cases the heuristic misses.

**3. Keep the skill, and put the rule where it always loads**

A one-line rule in the project's `CLAUDE.md` is loaded every session, so it doesn't depend on the skill being selected. The skill can hold the detailed pattern (schema location, error shape).

**Checking the diagnosis first**

Before you change anything, look at a failing session's transcript. If `Skill` was never invoked, the description isn't matching the task well enough. Make it name the trigger explicitly, for example "use when creating or editing any handler in src/api/". If the skill was invoked and the validation was still skipped, the skill was loaded but not followed, and only the hook and CI check will fix that.

file_path: skills/flaky-finder/SKILL.md
content:
---
name: flaky-finder
description: Find flaky tests by running the test suite three times and reporting the names of tests that failed in some runs but not others. Use when the user asks which tests are flaky, or to rerun the suite to find intermittent failures.
context: fork
allowed-tools: Bash(pnpm test) Bash(pnpm test *) Bash(mkdir *) Bash(grep *) Bash(wc *) Read
---

Find the flaky tests in this repository. Your reply is the only thing the main conversation sees, so keep it to the result.

The full test output is thousands of lines. Do not print it, and do not paste it into your reply. Read only the failure lines you need.

## Procedure

1. Create a fresh directory for this run: `mkdir -p "$TMPDIR/flaky-finder-$(date +%s)"`. Use that path as `RUN_DIR` for everything below.

2. Run the suite three times, one after another, never in parallel, so runs do not compete for resources and skew timing-sensitive tests. For each run `N` in 1, 2, 3:

   `pnpm test > "$RUN_DIR/run$N.log" 2>&1; echo "run $N exit $?"`

   Record each exit code. A non-zero exit means at least one test failed in that run. Do not stop early if a run fails; all three runs are needed.

3. For each log, identify the failing test names. Find the runner's failure summary first, because it lists each failed test once. Use `grep` with a narrow pattern to find it, for example `grep -n -E "FAIL|✕|✗|●|failing" "$RUN_DIR/run1.log"`. Work out which runner is in use (Jest, Vitest, Mocha, or other) from the output, then match its format. Extract the full test name, including the describe/suite path, so two tests with the same leaf name in different suites stay distinct.

   Write one normalized list per run to `$RUN_DIR/failed$N.txt`, one name per line, sorted and de-duplicated. Use `sort -u`. If the failure output for a run is unreadable, say so in your reply and do not guess names for that run.

4. Compute the flaky set: names that appear in at least one run's list and are missing from at least one other run's list. Use `comm` or `grep -vxF` against the other files. Do not count names that failed in all three runs. Those fail consistently, so they are not flaky.

5. Check the result. If a name appears in the flaky set, confirm it by grepping its line in the logs where it failed and where it passed. If you cannot confirm it, drop it and say so.

## Reply

Reply with only:

- The exit code of each run, on one line.
- The flaky test names, one per line, with the full describe/suite path. Nothing else around each name.
- If the flaky set is empty, say: `No flaky tests found: every failure was consistent across the three runs.`
- If a run's output could not be parsed, name that run and say why.
- The `RUN_DIR` path, so the user can read the full logs if they want to.

Do not add explanations, suggestions, or diagnoses of why each test is flaky. The user asked for names.

trajectory.body:
I made flaky-finder a skill, not a subagent: `skills/flaky-finder/SKILL.md`. It runs in its own context with `context: fork`, so the reruns' output never enters your conversation.

**Why a skill:** the work is a fixed procedure: three runs of `pnpm test`, then a diff of failure lists. An agent is for open-ended dispatch, a tool policy that must bind to everything it does, or parallel workers. None of those apply here. `context: fork` gives the isolation you need.

**What it does:**
- Runs `pnpm test` three times in sequence, not in parallel, so timing-sensitive tests aren't skewed by competing load. Each run's output goes to a log file under `$TMPDIR`.
- Extracts failing test names from each log's failure summary, keeping the describe/suite path so same-named tests in different suites stay distinct.
- Reports tests that failed in some runs but not others. Tests that failed in all three are excluded, since they fail consistently rather than flakily.
- The reply contains the three exit codes, the flaky names, and the log directory path. It has no diagnoses or commentary.

**Choices I made that you can redirect:**
- The runner is not named in the skill; it infers Jest, Vitest, or Mocha from the output. If the suite uses a different reporter, the name extraction is the part to adjust.
- Consistently failing tests are excluded. If you want them listed too, that's a one-line change.
- `allowed-tools` pre-approves only `pnpm test`, `mkdir`, `grep`, `wc`, and `Read`.

**Verification:** `claude-lint` reports 0 errors, 0 warnings, 0 info for the file. I did not run the skill end to end. This directory has no `package.json`, so `pnpm test` has nothing to run here. The plugin manifest also has no `skills/` directory until now, so I created it.
